get.description:
The plan is already computed before every rollback — this exposes the same
computation as a read, so an operator can see the change before committing to
it rather than discovering it afterwards. A rollback restores many values at
once from a state nobody has inspected and is the operation most likely to be
run under pressure; the one thing that makes that safe is being able to look
first.

Nothing is written, so there is no precondition and no audit record: this
answers a question rather than taking an action. Behind the same permission as
the rollback it previews, because a plan names every value that would change
and that is the same information.

post.description:
The order is deliberate and each step exists for a reason:

1. the precondition, so a rollback cannot be run from a page left open — the
   operation most likely to be attempted from one (ADR 0038);
2. the plan, computed without writing, because the keys a rollback touches are
   derived from history rather than submitted, and nothing can be authorized
   until they are known;
3. the same per-key permission check an ordinary write performs, which is what
   stops rollback becoming a way to change a guarded value without holding the
   permission that guards it;
4. the write, applying the plan that was authorized rather than a fresh one.

It reports what it restored and what it did not. A group containing a credential
is rolled back successfully and names that credential as unrestorable, because a
secret has no history to restore from — an operator gets a checklist rather than
a failure or a silence.
post.summary: Restore a group to the state it held at a point in its history (ADR 0040)

get.summary: List accounts

post.description:
A regular account, always. `users.create` has been in the catalogue and on the
seeded administrator role since Phase 6 with nothing serving it — a permission
describing an intention the platform ignored — and this is where it is served.
It does not become a second route across the administrative boundary:
AccountTypeManager remains the only one, so an administrator is still made by
creating an account and then promoting it, which needs `users.update` as well.

The address is not verified. Nothing here can confirm an address on somebody
else's behalf, and marking it verified because an administrator typed it would
make verification mean "an administrator typed it".
post.summary: Create an account

get.summary: Show a single account

put.description:
Identity only. What the account may do is changed through promotion, role
synchronisation and activation, each behind its own operation and its own
permission.

Changing the address clears its verification, and that is a security property
rather than an inconvenience: leaving `email_verified_at` set would let an
administrator move an account onto an address nobody has confirmed while the
platform went on treating it as confirmed — which for an administrative account
is the difference between a verified identity and an asserted one (ADR 0012).
The account verifies the new address through the normal flow.

post.summary: Let an account sign in again

post.description:
Existing tokens are revoked, matching promotion and demotion: the perimeter
refuses a suspended account on the next request either way, but a live token
belonging to an account that has been switched off is a loose end, and the two
operations that already change standing do not leave one.

An administrator cannot deactivate themselves. The platform would accept it and
the next request would be refused, leaving somebody locked out of the console
they were administering with no way back in from it — so it is refused here,
where the intent is still visible, rather than honoured and regretted.
post.summary: Stop an account signing in

because the whole point is that a person may have edited it before
deciding. Accepting something the platform did not propose is the normal
case, not an edge one.

AcceptSuggestionRequest.title: AcceptSuggestionRequest

AiCheckRequest.description:
What a connection test asks about.

With no body, the default provider is tested as saved. Naming a provider tests that
one; adding a key or a model tests the form as it stands, before anything is saved —
the key is used for this one call and never stored.

provider.description: The provider to test, by driver name. Absent means the default provider.

api_key.description: A key to test with instead of the stored one. Never stored.

model.description: A model to test with instead of the saved one.

AiCheckRequest.title: AiCheckRequest

AnnouncementAudience.description:
Who an announcement is addressed to. A closed set rather than a query an operator composes, and small on purpose. These are the two audiences the platform can describe without knowing what it is for: everyone who can sign in, and the people who run it. Anything narrower — a department, a cohort, a segment — is a property of an application built on this foundation and not of the foundation (ADR 0033). Suspended accounts are in neither. A message to an account that cannot sign in is a message nobody will read, and the in-app record is the channel this notification defaults to. | | |---| | `everyone`
Every active account, administrators included. | | `administrators`
Active administrative accounts only. |
AnnouncementAudience.title: AnnouncementAudience

action_label.description:
Beside the stable identifier, never instead of it (ADR 0031). The action
is what a client branches on; the label is what a person reads.

email_verified.description:
Both, and they answer different questions. A client branches on the
boolean — show the verification screen or do not — and an interface
showing an account renders the moment. Deriving the first from the
second in every client is how one of them ends up treating an empty
string as verified.

phone.description:
The account's own number, in full. It is theirs; the masking on the
verification endpoints exists because a *destination* echoed back is a
way of reading a number out of the platform, and this is not that.

roles.description:
Names, not identifiers. A permission's name is its stable contract and
what `can()` is asked with (ADR 0031); its row id is an implementation
detail of the vendor table it lives in.

EdgeInvalidationKind.description:
What an edge invalidation names (ADR 0036, ADR 0053). The five scopes every CDN this platform is likely to front offers in some form. A driver that cannot honour one says so, and the request is refused before it is queued rather than accepted and silently dropped. | | |---| | `urls`
Exact addresses, as the edge keyed them. | | `tags`
Every object the origin labelled with a tag (ADR 0053 §3). | | `prefixes`
Every object whose address starts with a prefix. | | `hosts`
Every object served for a host name. | | `everything`
Everything. An incident tool, never an invalidation strategy (ADR 0036). |
EdgeInvalidationKind.title: EdgeInvalidationKind

include_secrets.description:
Defaults to false when absent. Carrying ciphertext has to be asked for:
the safe artefact is the one that is worth less if it leaks, and an
operator who wanted the other one knows they did.

settings.description: Non-secret configuration, keyed by setting name.

credential_summary.description:
For a Firebase provider with a stored service account, the project it sends
through. Null for every other provider, and when nothing is stored.

captcha_token.description: The captcha response, when the platform is asking for one.

MediaAnalysisClassification.description: An advisory reading of an analysis's scores against the thresholds an operator set (ADR 0054). Advisory, and deliberately so. It is derived from the scores and the policy version recorded beside it; a consumer may use it, or apply its own threshold to the scores, or ignore both. It is null when no thresholds are configured, because a classification nobody defined would be the platform inventing a decision.
MediaAnalysisClassification.title: MediaAnalysisClassification

scores.description: A score between 0 and 1 for each type the analyzer assessed. A type it did not assess is absent, never 0.

MediaAnalysisReviewDecision.description: What a person concluded after reading an analysis (ADR 0054). A review never edits the analysis it is about. It is recorded beside it, attributed and audited, so the analyzer's reading and the person's stay distinguishable forever.
MediaAnalysisReviewDecision.title: MediaAnalysisReviewDecision

MediaAnalysisStatus.description:
Where one media analysis stands (ADR 0054). Only `completed` and `inconclusive` are assessments. `failed`, `unsupported` and `cancelled` say nothing about the media at all — and none of them, `inconclusive` included, means the media is authentic. A consumer that reads any of them as "human" is making a claim no analyzer supported. | | |---| | `pending`
| | `processing`
| | `completed`
The analyzer returned scores for at least one requested type. | | `inconclusive`
The analyzer ran and could not reach an assessment. | | `unsupported`
The analyzer ran and supports none of the requested types for this media. | | `failed`
The analysis could not be carried out. | | `cancelled`
Withdrawn before it ran, or stopped because the capability or the media went away. |
MediaAnalysisStatus.title: MediaAnalysisStatus

MediaAnalysisType.description:
What a media analysis can be asked to look for (ADR 0054). The vocabulary is closed and owned here, so a consumer chooses from it and cannot invent a type an analyzer would not recognise. An analyzer declares the subset it supports; a type it does not support is reported as unsupported, never scored as zero. Every type names an indicator of risk. None of them is a verdict: an analyzer can say a video carries signs of generation, and cannot say that it was or was not generated. | | |---| | `ai_generated`
Signs that the media was produced by a generative model. | | `deepfake`
Signs of a synthetic likeness of a real person. | | `face_manipulation`
Signs that a face was swapped, re-enacted or altered. | | `visual_manipulation`
Signs that frames were edited, spliced or composited. | | `synthetic_audio`
Signs that speech or sound was synthesised. |
MediaAnalysisType.title: MediaAnalysisType

MediaStatus.description: Where a file is in its intake lifecycle. Verification is deliberately absent: whether an analyzer has looked at a file is independent of whether the file is usable, and coupling them would make readiness hostage to a capability most media never needs.
MediaStatus.title: MediaStatus

MediaType.description: The broad kind of a file, derived from its detected content type.
MediaType.title: MediaType

MediaVisibility.description: Whether a file is reachable without authorization. Deliberately only two values. Who is entitled to a private file is a business question that Media cannot answer — owner, team member, judge, subscriber — so it is delegated to a MediaAccessPolicy the attaching module supplies. Media knows whether authorization is required, never who satisfies it.
MediaVisibility.title: MediaVisibility

code.description: Wide enough for a 6-digit TOTP or a grouped recovery code.

NotificationChannel.description:
A route a notification can take to a recipient. Only channels the platform can actually deliver on exist here. Push arrived with the Integration capability it needed (ADR 0045); WhatsApp arrives when its own does (ADR 0017). | | |---| | `database`
| | `mail`
| | `sms`
| | `push`
A registered device (ADR 0045). What travels is a type and a record id — the device fetches the message over the authenticated API, because a push payload passes through Google and Apple and a lock screen is a public surface. |
NotificationChannel.title: NotificationChannel

locale.description: The language this message was rendered in when it was raised.

read_at.description:
Null until the recipient has read it. Reported as a moment rather than a
flag because an interface showing an inbox renders when, and a client
that only needs whether can compare against null.

NotificationType.description: The registry of notifications the platform can raise. Preferences reference this rather than free text, so a stored preference always names something real and a renamed notification cannot leave orphaned rows behind that silently mean nothing.
NotificationType.title: NotificationType

name.description: Needed only when the number has no account yet; the account is created with it.

RegisterPushDeviceRequest.description: A device asking to be reachable.

token.description:
The vendor's registration token. Long, and lengthened by vendors before
now, so the ceiling is generous rather than exact.

device_id.description:
Generated and kept by the client. This is what makes a token replaceable
rather than additive: FCM rotates tokens, and without a stable handle for
the handset a rotation leaves two rows and delivers twice.

label.description:
What a person would recognise in a list of their own devices. Display
only, and never trusted for anything else.

RegisterPushDeviceRequest.title: RegisterPushDeviceRequest

phone.description: Stored unverified; confirm it through phone verification.

types.description: What to look for, from the platform's vocabulary. Types the configured analyzer does not support are reported, not scored.

reanalyze.description: Run again even when an equivalent analysis exists; the new one supersedes the current one when it finishes.

RequestSuggestionsRequest.description: Ask for translations of what is missing in one language.

locale.description:
Checked against the platform's active languages by the controller. The
shape is all that is asserted here.

source.description:
Narrow to one body of content, or one item within it. Absent means
everything the caller may write.

include_translated.description:
Off by default, and deliberately: asking for a language means filling
the gaps. Paying a vendor to replace text a person already wrote is a
request an operator makes on purpose.

RequestSuggestionsRequest.title: RequestSuggestionsRequest

location.description:
A path on the configured disk, constrained so it cannot climb out of it.
The disk is where the deployment's own access controls apply; a location
that could contain "../" would let a restore read whatever the process can.

note.description: The reviewer's reasoning. Kept with the review; the audit trail records only that one was given.

label.description:
`label` is what an administrator types, and it is named for what it
is: the response's `name` is the machine identifier, so reusing that
word here would give one field two meanings across the same
resource. The identifier is derived from this server-side and is
immutable afterwards (ADR 0029 item 12), so this carries no
identifier grammar and no uniqueness rule — two roles may read the
same in a list while remaining distinct underneath.

items.description:
Only catalogued permissions may be attached, so a role cannot be given
a permission string the platform does not actually enforce anywhere. The
catalogue includes every module's registered permissions (ADR 0052).

name.description:
`name` is the immutable machine identifier and does not move.
`name_label` sits beside it (ADR 0031) so a client never has to
infer a human label from the identifier.

credential.description:
Required and non-empty. Rotation replaces a credential with another one;
emptying a secret is a different operation with a different audit action,
and ADR 0038 is explicit that a failed rotation must never leave the
field empty — the surest way to honour that is to have no path here that
could empty it.

SaveAiProviderRequest.description:
One AI provider's configuration, as the setup form submits it.

The API key is its own named field rather than an entry in a credential map, so an
administrator never needs to know what the driver calls it. Leaving it out keeps the
stored key; it is never read back. Nothing about how the driver reaches the vendor —
an address, a header — is accepted: that belongs to the driver.

api_key.description: The vendor's API key. Omit it to keep the key already stored.

model.description: The model this provider answers with.

SaveAiProviderRequest.title: SaveAiProviderRequest

ScanStatus.description: What a malware scanner concluded, if one ran. NOT_SCANNED exists so the platform never claims a guarantee nobody checked. No antivirus is available in this environment, so the null driver records this rather than CLEAN: a row asserting cleanliness on the strength of a scanner that did not run would be worse than an honest absence.
ScanStatus.title: ScanStatus

subject.description: The line a recipient sees first.

body.description:
What the announcement says. Substituted literally: a value is never
itself treated as a placeholder.

audience.description:
Who receives it. | | |---| | `everyone`
Every active account, administrators included. | | `administrators`
Active administrative accounts only. |

phone.description: The number to sign in or register with, with its country code.

reach.description:
Who reads this, and the sentence saying so. An operator reasonably
assumes a control that can be changed does something; a third of this
catalogue was declared ahead of the thing that would read it, and a
screen that does not say which is which is lying by omission.

default.description:
The default a fresh installation received. Never sent for a secret,
which by construction has none (ADR 0018).

depends_on.description:
What must be configured before this one takes effect, so an interface
can say so rather than letting an operator switch on something that
silently does nothing.

rules.description:
The rules this value must satisfy, as declared. Published because they
are enforced (Phase 16B-6): a client that generates a form from this
catalogue and does not know them will submit values the API refuses, and
an operator will read that as the platform being broken. Laravel rule strings, deliberately. Translating them into some neutral
schema here would invent a second dialect for the same constraints, and
the two would drift in exactly the direction that makes the client more
permissive than the server.

permission.description:
The permission required to change this setting, resolved rather than
repeated: `requiredPermission()` answers `settings.secrets.manage` for a
secret, which the raw declaration does not carry. Publishing the raw
field would show every credential as freely editable — and it is the
resolved answer the API itself enforces, so it is the one a client must
be given.

redirect_uri.description: Must be one of the redirect URIs an operator allowed, exactly.

items.description: What to purge: absolute URLs, tags, absolute URL prefixes or host names. Absent for everything.

reason.description: Why, in the operator's words. Kept on each purge request and in the audit trail.

confirm.description: Purging everything only: the verified scope's name, typed out.

file.description:
The file to upload. Its size must be within the maximum this platform is
configured to accept.

phone.description:
The account's phone number. Stored canonically; the lookup hash is
derived from it and is never accepted from outside.

password.description:
The account's first password. Must be confirmed, and must meet the
minimum length this platform is configured to require.

locale.description:
The language a localized value lands in. Absent means the request's own. The content language, which is not the console's display language: an
operator reading the console in Arabic may write the English site name,
and `X-Locale` cannot carry both meanings (ADR 0030).

settings.description: Non-secret configuration, keyed by setting name. Sending null clears every setting.

credentials.description: Vendor credentials, keyed by credential name. Omitting the field leaves the stored credentials untouched; sending null clears them. They are never read back.

service_account_json.description:
A Google service-account file, pasted whole. Firebase providers only. It
replaces the stored credentials in full, and only the project, the client
address and the private key are kept. Remove credentials with
`credentials: null`; omitting this leaves them as they are.

url.description:
ClientUrlPolicy's web-page rule: https in production, no credentials, no
fragment, never this machine.

current_password.description: Required when the account already has a password.

phone.description: A new number is stored unverified. Null removes it.

The account's phone number, or null to remove it. Stored canonically;
the lookup hash is derived and is never accepted from outside.

preferred_locale.description:
The language the platform addresses this account in. Constrained to the
languages table, so a preference can never name one the platform does
not serve.

phone.description: The account's phone number in canonical form, or null.

phone_verified.description:
Whether anybody has answered a code sent to it, and when. Reported the
same way the address is, and for the same reason: an interface showing
an account renders the moment, and a client that only needs the boolean
should not have to derive it from a null nobody documented.

email_verified.description: Whether the address has been confirmed, and when.

mfa_enrolled.description: Whether a confirmed second factor exists. Which one is not published.

has_linked_social_identity.description:
Whether a social identity can sign in to this account today. While true the
account cannot be promoted; identities unlinked in the past do not count.

linked_social_providers.description: The providers linked today. Never an identity's subject or address.

code.description: The code delivered by SMS.

WriteTranslationRequest.description: One item's translated fields, in one language.

locale.description:
Checked against the platform's active languages by the controller. The
shape is all that is asserted here — a locale that exists is a question
about data, not about the payload.

WriteTranslationRequest.title: WriteTranslationRequest

errors.description: A detailed description of each field that failed validation.
